What every host needs to operate

To talk on an IP network, every host must have:

  • A unique IP.
  • The subnet mask.
  • The default gateway, if we want to leave the network.
  • A DNS server.

Addresses used to be tracked by manual control, machine by machine. A mistake in the mask left the host disconnected, because it could not determine which network it belonged to.
Without those four items the host does not operate; entering them by hand does not scale and is a source of errors.
A server that hands out the configuration

DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) automates address distribution. It derives from BOOTP, which allowed initializing computers without a hard drive.

The server centralizes assignment and records which IP each client has. Advantages:

  • No need to keep the records by hand and no configuration errors.
  • A change is made on the server and everyone picks it up on their own.
  • IPs that are no longer used are reclaimed for another host.
  • All the parameters come along with the IP.
Dynamic assignment: addresses are lent for a while and return to the server.

The DHCP client runs on every device (PC, printer, TV). On initialization it has no IP and does not know who the server is, so it uses special addresses:

  • Source IP 0.0.0.0.
  • Destination IP 255.255.255.255 (broadcast): it reaches everyone, and there may be several servers.

The Discover carries the client's MAC and its name. It is sent when first powering on, when the server rejects a request, or when the client releases its IP and asks for a new one.
It is a broadcast: the switch delivers it out of all its ports. Only DHCP servers will answer it.
2 · Offer: each server makes its offer

All DHCP servers that receive the request answer with an offer:

  • The client's MAC (which still has IP 0.0.0.0).
  • The offered IP and the mask.
  • The lease: how long the assignment lasts.
  • The server identification (its IP).

Each server reserves the address it offered while it waits for confirmation. If several offers arrive, the client has to pick one (generally the first).

The client picks an offer and sends a Request: it asks that server to let it keep the offered address.

Since it still has no IP to operate with, the exchange remains broadcast. This has an advantage: all servers find out which offer was accepted. The one that was not chosen releases the address it had reserved.
The broadcast Request accepts one offer and, along the way, tells the other servers theirs is now free.

The server whose offer was accepted answers with a positive confirmation: the ACK. It contains the assigned IP and the other configuration parameters.

Only at that moment can the client start using the address.

The server does not verify that the client is really using it: it just hands it out, and through the lease it knows when it will be available again.
When the answer is no: NACK and other messages

The server can answer a Request with a NACK: it does not confirm the address. This happens when:

  • The client tries to renew a previous IP (skipping Discover and Offer) and it is no longer available.
  • The IP is invalid because the client physically moved to another subnet.

Other client messages: Decline (the address is already in use; it detects this with gratuitous ARP), Release (releases the assignment and cancels the lease), and Inform (asks only for additional parameters).

At 50% of the lease the client tries to renew. With 24 h, it does so at 12 h. It needs no Discover or Offer because its IP is still valid: it sends a Request, and with the ACK it has another 24 h.

If the server does not respond, it retries at half of what remains: 6 h later and, a third and last time, 3 h later. With no confirmation (or with a NACK) it releases the IP and goes back to Discover.
If the machine is disconnected there is no renewal: once the lease runs out, the server reclaims the address.
Designing the service: pools, options, and lease

• Split the space between two DHCP servers: without an IP, the client cannot operate.
  • Exclude from the pool a range for static IPs (routers, printers).
  • Configure the routers to let DHCP requests through, which are broadcast.
  • DDNS: if a station changes IP, the IP–name relationship must be updated.

Options (RFC 2132) allow sending more parameters so the client configures itself.
Small pool → short lease: addresses are reclaimed quickly and can be lent again.
Last octet: who hands out each range
Static: routers, printers, and other devices you want to always find at the same IP.
Two servers: if one goes down, the other keeps handing out addresses from its part of the space.
With no free addresses, the server makes no offer. With a small pool, a short lease leaves some margin.

• Discover: broadcast from 0.0.0.0 with MAC and name.
  • Offer: IP, mask, lease, and server id; the IP stays reserved.
  • Request: in broadcast; the other servers release their offer.
  • ACK: the IP can now be used. NACK: back to Discover.
  • Renewal at 50% of the lease.

The client does not have an IP yet (0.0.0.0) and does not know who the server is, so it looks for it by broadcast.
Why is the Request sent as broadcast even though the client has already chosen a server?
Because the switch does not know where the server is
So the other servers know which offer was accepted and release theirs
So all hosts update their ARP table
Because DHCP does not support any other kind of delivery
The client still operates without an IP, and broadcast lets the servers that were not chosen reclaim the address they had reserved.
A client gets an IP with a 24 h lease. When does it first try to renew it?
Renewal is attempted at 50% of the lease; if there is no response, it retries 6 h later and then 3 h later.
The address pool is small relative to the number of machines that pass through the network. What is best?
A long lease, to renew less often
A short lease, to reclaim addresses quickly
